analysis.one_liner: Requires airlines to pay passengers up to $775 for delays and cancellations the airline caused.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the House in December 2025 with five Democratic cosponsors and sent to the Aviation Subcommittee in February 2026; no hearing or vote has been scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill directs the Transportation Secretary to write rules requiring airlines to compensate passengers for significant delays or cancellations caused by the airline itself. Passengers arriving 3 to 9 hours late could get up to $300, and those arriving 9 or more hours late up to $775, plus free rebooking if a missed connection leaves them stranded. The payments are separate from the refunds airlines must already issue for canceled or significantly changed flights.
analysis.who_benefits: Air travelers whose flights are delayed or canceled for reasons within the airline's control — things like crew shortages, maintenance problems, or scheduling decisions. Today they are entitled to a refund of the unused ticket but not to cash compensation for lost time, missed events, or hotel and meal costs; this bill would create a guaranteed payment on top of the refund. The 3-hour threshold covers the most common damaging delays, and the free-rebooking requirement protects people whose missed connection leaves them stuck partway through a trip.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Air travelers hit by airline-caused delays

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Transportation Secretary, within one year of enactment, to write rules obligating airlines to pay passengers up to $300 when an airline-caused delay or cancellation means arriving 3 to 9 hours late, and up to $775 for arrivals 9 or more hours late [S2].
When a delay or cancellation causes a passenger to miss a connecting flight, the airline must book them on the next available flight at no additional cost [S2].

The compensation requirement applies to both domestic and international flights operated by U.S. air carriers and is written as a separate obligation from existing refund requirements, so airlines could not substitute a refund for the cash payment [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Airlines, and by extension their shareholders, would bear the cost of the payments and rebookings. Airlines would likely pass some of the cost into ticket prices, and carriers that operate with chronically tight schedules would face the largest exposure. Passengers delayed by weather or air traffic control problems — events outside the airline's control — would get nothing under this bill, which is the standard compromise in these proposals but leaves many stranded travelers uncovered.

drawbacks.text: The compensation is a ceiling, not a floor: the bill says 'not more than' $300 or $775, leaving the Transportation Secretary discretion to set the required amounts lower through the rulemaking process, so travelers may end up with less than the headline numbers [S2].

The payments cover only delays or cancellations within the airline's control, so passengers stranded by weather or air traffic control disruptions — some of the worst travel meltdowns — get no compensation under this bill [S2].

A flat payment may not match actual losses: a $775 payment can exceed what a budget traveler lost, while a business traveler who missed a day of a week-long international trip may lose far more, meaning the cap both under- and over-compensates [S2].
Airlines would face a new ongoing cost, and some of it would likely be recovered through fares, so infrequent flyers who never experience a delay would help subsidize payments to those who do [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: This is a genuine, targeted consumer protection: it converts 'sorry, here's your refund' into a real penalty airlines can feel, which is the main lever for improving on-time performance. The caps are modest by international standards — the European Union pays up to roughly $650 on shorter routes regardless of the ticket price — and the Secretary's discretion to set lower amounts weakens the guarantee. The exclusion of weather delays is defensible but leaves the biggest meltdown scenarios uncovered. On balance the benefit to travelers outweighs the cost, which is modest and partly passed into fares.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in mid-December 2025 and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which sent it to its Aviation Subcommittee in early February 2026; it has not had a hearing, markup, or vote, and the 119th Congress is still in session.

narrative.text: Rep. Emilia Sykes of Ohio introduced the Airline Passenger Compensation Act of 2025 in the House on December 17, 2025 [S1] [S4].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure the day it was introduced, and on February 2, 2026 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Aviation [S4].
Four Democratic colleagues — Reps. Rick Larsen of Washington, Greg Stanton of Arizona, Andre Carson of Indiana, and Julie Johnson of Texas — joined as cosponsors; no Republican has signed on [S3].
No further action has been taken since the subcommittee referral, and no committee vote or floor vote has been scheduled [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything on the merits. Airlines keep operating under the current rules, where a refund of the unused ticket is the only guaranteed remedy for a canceled flight, because no compensation requirement has advanced. Travelers on airline-caused delayed flights continue to bear their own costs for meals, hotels, and missed connections.

for.name: Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on December 17, 2025 and became its lead sponsor.

for.name: Reps. Rick Larsen, Greg Stanton, Andre Carson, and Julie Johnson
for.what_they_did: Joined as the bill's four cosponsors, all Democrats, at introduction.

for.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
for.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and referred it to the Subcommittee on Aviation on February 2, 2026 — the standard first step, which so far has not led to a hearing.

against.name: Airlines for America and the major U.S. carriers
against.what_they_did: The airline industry has publicly opposed mandatory cash compensation for delays during the Transportation Department's rulemaking on the same subject, arguing automatic payments would raise fares.

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled a hearing or markup on the bill in the two months since it was referred to the Aviation Subcommittee.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a Democrat — five House Democrats in total — and no Republican has signed on, so the bill's visible support splits entirely by party [S3].

industries.note: The bill creates a new mandatory cash payout — up to $300 or $775 per affected passenger — plus free rebooking for missed connections, payable whenever the airline itself causes a significant delay or cancellation. Airlines lose a stream of payments they do not owe today, and their financial interest in the bill runs against travelers' interest in being compensated for lost time.
A guaranteed airline payment for airline-caused disruptions reduces the need for some travelers to buy trip-delay coverage, shrinking a market built partly on gaps the bill would close.

analysis.trajectory: Bills with a handful of cosponsors that sit in a subcommittee without a hearing rarely reach the floor. The bill has no Republican support, and the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee's agenda is controlled by the majority party. Unless the Aviation Subcommittee holds a hearing or the Department of Transportation finalizes its own compensation rule and builds momentum, this bill is likely to expire at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
